ARTICLE IN PRESS The ritual stance affects perceptions of effort Abstract Cognitive theories of ritual propose that ceremonial actions are processed through a distinct “ritual stance,” which emphasizes symbolic and social value over utilitarian demands. We tested whether this stance alters perceptions of costs and benefits by presenting 289 Hindu participants in Mauritius with vignettes describing identical activities—carrying, cooking, fasting, and walking—framedS either in ritual or ordinary S contexts. Participants rated each activity on perceived difficulty and happiness during and E R after completion. Linear mixed models showed that ritual framing reduced perceived P difficulty by an average of 11% and increased happiness ratings by 25% during and 18% N I after the activity compared to the same actions performed in a utilitarian context, E suggesting that the ritual stance iLntroduces a distinct set of cognitive biases that affect C decision-making. Group contIexts enhanced these effects. These findings demonstrate T that the ritual stance funRctions as a cognitive heuristic that reappraises costs in symbolic A terms, thereby lowering perceived barriers to participation in demanding practices. Beyond their cognitive implications, these results shed light on the cultural and evolutionary dynamics of ritual, including their potential role in motivating costly cooperative behaviors and their broader applicability in reframing everyday challenges. 1. Introduction Cognitive theories of ritual argue that ceremonial actions are processed in psychologically 1 ARTICLE IN PRESS distinct ways compared to ordinary, utilitarian actions (Herrmann et al., 2013; Whitehouse, 2021). According to this view, each type of action is learned and understood through a different cognitive lens. On the one hand, utilitarian actions are interpreted on the basis of an “instrumental stance”, which seeks out a rationale for these actions related to principles of physical causality. On the other hand, causally opaque, ceremonial actions are interpreted through a “ritual stance”, in which the interpreter seeks out explanations based on social normativity and cultural convention. Notably, the distinction between these two cognitivSe stances does not merely S depend on whether causal explanations are accessible to the interpreter. That is, even E R when the underlying causal mechanisms of instrumental actions are unknown, there is P still an expectation that such mechanisms exist; that they operate in line with natural laws; N I and that they are in principle knowable (Xygalatas, 2022b). Thus, when we use a remote E control to turn on the television, weL may not possess all the relevant technical knowledge C to understand how this actioIn relates to its end goal (e.g. exactly how the mechanical T motion of pressing a bRutton ultimately results into specific patterns of photons being A emitted from the screen), but we nonetheless trust that there is a causal chain of events that leads to this outcome. When it comes to ritual actions, however, their effects cannot be described or inferred in terms of physical causality, as there is no causal link between the action performed (e.g. pouring drops of oil into a bowl of water) and its end goal (e.g. healing a headache inflicted by the evil eye) (Xygalatas, 2021). Therefore, the inner workings of ritual actions are in principle unknowable (Legare & Souza, 2012, 2014). What is more, the distinction between the instrumental and the ritual stance cannot be drawn with reference to the actions themselves, as the same behavior (e.g. food 2 ARTICLE IN PRESS preparation), can be instrumental in one case (eating a meal) and ceremonial (making a sacrifice) in another (Legare & Herrmann, 2013; Willard et al., 2023). Thus, distinguishing between the two requires interpretation based on situational and socio-cultural cues. That is, ritual actions are causally opaque, conventional, and normative. We argue that the ritual stance operates as a cognitive shortcut that simplifies the processing of ritualized actions by reappraising their costs and benefits, upweighting their symbolic and social value while downplaying their utilitarian demands. This heuristic allows individuals to quickly evaluate socially sanctionedS behaviors based on their S emotional payoff without computing detailed causal or energetic accounts. In the context E R of decision-making, adopting the ritual stance may enable individuals to navigate social P complexities with reduced cognitive effort, by aligning themselves with group expectations N I and thus reaping the benefits of group membership. E Empirical research supportLs the idea that ritual actions are perceived in distinct C ways. For example, studies Ion action-parsing show that non-instrumental (ritualistic) T behaviors are treated bRy observers as more fine-grained, independent series of actions A rather than longer, logically interconnected steps and are described in greater detail compared to instrumental actions (Nielbo et al., 2012; Nielbo & Sørensen, 2011). Moreover, in contrast to instrumental behaviors, ritual actions are seen as being their own goal rather than merely a means to an end (Liberman et al., 2018; Schachner & Carey, 2013). Due to their normative nature, ritual actions are also perceived to be socially meaningful (Liberman et al., 2018; Schachner & Carey, 2013). Studies with children show that they eagerly adopt the ceremonial behaviors of their peers, which they imitate with greater precision than they do instrumental actions (Clegg & Legare, 2016; Nielsen et al., 3 ARTICLE IN PRESS 2015, 2018; Wilks et al., 2016), and expect others to do so as well (Nielsen, 2018; Rakoczy et al., 2008). Given the above, it is no surprise that ritual actions are intuitively interpreted as significant. For instance, studies show that objects handled in ritualistic ways are judged to be more valuable and desirable compared to the same objects presented in ordinary ways (Kapitány & Nielsen, 2015), and actions that are more ritualized are judged to have greater efficacy (Legare & Souza, 2012; Xygalatas, Maňo, & Pinto, 2021). Thus, rituals imbue actions with meaning, making them feel special and Smore rewarding compared to S instrumental actions. E R These findings are also in accordance with ethnographic observations. P Practitioners commonly describe cultural rituals as an important and indispensable part N I of their personal and collective identity (Xygalatas, 2013). But when ethnographers ask E them about the purpose of these acLtions, they often indicate that performing the ceremony C is done for its own sake – it isI an end in itself (Xygalatas & Maňo, 2022). In other words, T rituals are described Ras autotelic experiences (Csikszentmihalyi, 1990), which are A perceived as highly significant and intrinsically motivating. Evolutionary theories highlight the important role of rituals in human societies (Atran & Henrich, 2010; Henrich, 2009; Xygalatas, 2023). Ceremonial practices play a crucial role in transmitting cultural knowledge, norms, and values across generations (Boyd & Richerson, 1988) and maintaining social order (Turner, 1995). These practices involve high-fidelity imitation (Lyons et al., 2007), which is facilitated by cultural learning mechanisms such as conformity bias and prestige bias, prompting individuals to preferentially adopt behaviors that are common within their group or demonstrated by 4 ARTICLE IN PRESS high-status individuals (Henrich & McElreath, 2003). This tendency is adaptive, because it ensures the faithful adoption and transmission of complex behaviors and social norms, even when the underlying causal mechanisms are not fully understood (Legare & Nielsen, 2015). Cultural learning biases help individuals navigate the vast array of information and behaviors in their environment by providing heuristics for what to learn and whom to learn from (Boyd & Richerson, 1985). This selective imitation is crucial for the efficient transmission of cultural knowledge, as it allows individualsS to adopt socially beneficial S practices without expending resources to understand their causal structure (Mesoudi, E R 2011). The ritual stance leverages these biases by shifting attention towards the symbolic P benefits of participation and reducing the salience of its material and emotional demands. N I Thus, by underestimating the physical or mental costs associated with ritual participation, E individuals are more likely to engaLge in group rituals that demand substantial costs (e.g., C fasting, long pilgrimages, orI physical endurance tasks). If these actions were judged T based on their objectivRe difficulty, participation rates might be lower, undermining the A group’s ability to create cohesion and shared identity. The heuristic minimizes perceived barriers, making it easier for individuals to commit to group activities. In the current study, we examined whether the ritual stance alters perceptions of physical and emotional costs associated with particular actions. To do this, we presented participants with a series of culturally relevant vignettes about people performing the same actions either in a ritual setting (e.g. a 36-hour fast for religious reasons) or a non- ritual setting (a 36-hour fast for health reasons) and asked them to estimate how they would feel about it. We hypothesized that the ritual stance would affect judgments of 5 ARTICLE IN PRESS difficulty, such that when the same action is performed in a ceremonial setting, it would be perceived as easier, as well as judgments of happiness, such that when the same action is performed in a ceremonial setting, it would be perceived as more rewarding. 2. Ethnographic context The study was conducted in Mauritius, an Indian Ocean nation which is one of the world’s three countries with a Hindu plurality. Unlike the other two (India and Nepal), however, Mauritius has a more diverse religious landscape, with sSizable Christian and Muslim S populations, while numerous other religions are represented. Overall, Hindus make up E R just under half of the Mauritian population. Moreover, there is significant cultural exchange P between ethno-religious groups, which results in various syncretic forms of worship N I (Klocová et al., 2022), while conversion is also relatively common. E Mauritian Hindus practice La great diversity of rituals, many of which involve C substantial costs that may taIke the form of time investments, abstinence from food and T pleasure, or intense phRysical exertion. Examples relevant to this study include the Maha A Shivaratri (Great night of Shiva), a long pilgrimage that involves walking long distances to visit a sacred lake in the heart of the island; and the Thaipusam Kavadi, where devotees pierce their bodies and carry heavy offerings to the temple of Murugan; in addition to these focal activities, many Hindu festivals include fasting for several days, which is then concluded with collective meals cooked by members of the devotees’ families. 3. Participants We recruited 319 Mauritian individuals (190 reported their sex as female, 128 male, and 1 as “other”) ages 18-83 (mean age =36.94, SD=14.83) in a variety of urban and rural areas in the districts of Port Louis, Black River, Plaines Wilhems, Moka, Pamplemousses, Rivière du Rempart, Flacq, and Savanne, covering 8 of the 9 administrative districts of the island (figure 1). Participants were approached by local research assistants in a variety of public settings, including universities, marketplaces, parks, and bus stations, who asked them to take part iSn a brief survey about how S individuals evaluate other people’s experiences. As our study focused on Hindu rituals, E R we aimed to specifically recruit Hindus. However, 24 participants self-identified as P Muslims and six as Christian. Those individuals were excluded from the analysis, leaving N I a total of 289 subjects. Notably, four of the remaining subjects also reported practicing E another religion in addition to HindLuism, which is not uncommon in Mauritius. Materials and Procedures The survey was administered by the first author or one of the local assistants in 8 ARTICLE IN PRESS either English or Mauritian Creole, based on each participant’s preference (Mauritius is a multilingual country). Each participant read seven short vignettes about a person engaged in a particular activity and answered three questions about each person’s experience. Specifically, they were asked: (1) How happy did this person feel during the process? (2) How happy did this person feel after the process? (3) How difficult was the process for this person? The questions were presented in an 11-point Visual Analog Scale (VAS) ranging from 0 being “not happy at all” to 10 being “extremely happy”, and from 0 being “not difficult at all” to 10 being “extremely difficult” respectiveSly. S All vignettes were selected through conversations with the local research E R assistants, who helped us choose examples that were salient for the local population. The P first three vignettes were the same across all participants and served as practice items. N I These vignettes presented simple scenarios such as “On a Saturday morning, a man had E a flat tire. He had to change it.” L C The four subsequent Ivignettes each belonged to either a ritual or a non-ritual T condition, presented in Rrandom order. In the ritual condition, the activity in question was A practiced in the context of a well-known religious ceremony of the local community. For example, “On the day of Thaipusam, a man is walking to the local temple. He is carrying a kavadi that weighs 20 kg.” (the Thaipusam is a religious festival that involves carrying heavy offerings called kavadi in a long procession). In the non-ritual condition, the person engaged in a similar activity outside of the ritual context. For example, “On a Tuesday morning, a man is walking to his stall in the market. He is carrying a crate of mangoes that weighs 20 kg.” Within each condition, we also varied the type, intensity, and social setting of the 9 ARTICLE IN PRESS activity. Specifically, each participant was presented with 4 types of activities: carrying, cooking, fasting, and walking. Similar to the example above, cooking to feed 30 guests at home (non-ritual) was matched to cooking to feed 30 ritual participants at the temple (ritual); a 36-hour fast for health reasons was matched to a 36-hour fast for religious reasons; and walking 12 km because one’s bus broke down was matched to walking 12 km in the context of a religious pilgrimage. As a validity check, each activity was presented either in a high- or low-intensity version: carrying 5kg or 20 kg; cooking for 8 or 30 people; fasting for 12 or 36 hours; and walking for 5 km or 12 km. S S Finally, each activity described the person performing the same action either alone E R or in the company of more people, e.g. “a man and his friends…”. Previous research P suggests that social context may modulate perceptions of effort. For instance, participants N I in an experiment estimated a hill to be less steep when they were in another person’s E company compared to being aloLne (Schnall et al., 2008). Similar results have been C obtained in studies that examIined experiences rather than expectations, showing that T social support can attenRuate feelings of effort or pain (Davis et al., 2021; Roberts et al., A 2015; Stevens et al., 2020). As most cultural rituals are collective, this variable was used to account for such contextual factors. All permutations were fully randomized, and each combination (e.g. ritual/walking/alone/high intensity) was presented only once for each participant. After seeing each vignette, participants were asked the same 3 questions about how happy the protagonist felt during and after the activity and how difficult the task was. In addition to their responses to the vignette scenarios, we also asked participants to identify their age, sex, religious affiliation, religiosity, and frequency of ritual attendance. 10 ARTICLE IN PRESS Religiosity was assessed on a 4-point scale (“how religious do you consider yourself?”) ranging from 1 “not at all” to 4 “extremely”. Ritual frequency was assessed by an open- ended question “How often do you attend religious rituals?”, and answers were coded on a 4-point scale (0=Never; 1=At least once a year; 2=At least once a month; 3=At least once a week). Data were collected on tablet computers and participants completed the survey with the assistance of the researchers, who were available to answer questions during the study. S S 4. Results E R Data were analyzed using R 4.1 (R Core Team, 2021). An Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) P and post hoc tests with Bonferroni corrections showed that of the four types of activities N I cooking, fasting, and carrying were perceived similarly, but the fourth (walking) was seen E as more difficult and less pleasurabLle compared to the other activities. This is unsurprising C based on our experience doinIg fieldwork in Mauritius, where walking long distances was T not very common and, Rwhen asked for directions, people would often refer to relatively A small distances as being too far to cover on foot. For the main analysis, we used Linear Mixed Models to fit a series of regressions on our dependent variables while adjusting for the random effects of subject ID and activity type. We present three models for each dependent variable: first, a basic model including the main predictors: ritual vs non-ritual, individual vs group, and high vs low intensity; second, an expanded model adjusted for demographic variables. Those include age, sex, religiosity, and ritual frequency. Finally, subsequent models included interactions between condition (Ritual) and the religious variables (Religiosity; Ritual 11 ARTICLE IN PRESS Attendance). To avoid issues of collinearity, as religious belief and ritual attendance are closely linked, we included only one of these two variables at a time. In line with our prediction, we found that the same activities performed in a ritual context were perceived as less difficult and were associated with more happiness both during and after completing the action compared to a non-ritual context (figure 2). Moreover, the same activities were perceived as less difficult and were associated with more happiness when performed in a group context compared to being performed alone. These results were robust to the effects of demographic facStors, of which only age had a S consistent effect on ratings, such that younger participants rated the same activities as E R more difficult and less pleasurable compared to older ones. There was also a trend P towards more perceived happiness and less perceived difficulty for more religious N I individuals. Although this trend did not reach significance, it may have been because the E effect of Ritual on judgments was Lstronger for more religious people (Table 1). Discussion Our findings reveal that identical actions are perceived as less difficult and more happiness-inducing when framed in a ritual context, demonstrating the role of the ritual stance as a cognitive shortcut that allows individuals to reappraise those actions through a value-based re-weighting lens. While people still register effort—more intense actions were unsurprisingly judged as more effortful—they appear to give it less momentary weight relative to the symbolic and social value highlighted by the ritual frame. 16 ARTICLE IN PRESS Notably, the perceptual shift associated with the ritual condition was similar to or greater than that associated with substantially lowering the intensity of the action. For example, the ritual condition was associated with an average decrease of approximately 11% on the difficulty scale, which was comparable to the decrease associated with the low-intensity condition (13.6%). In our vignettes, these differences in intensity represented carrying one-quarter of the weight; cooking for about one-quarter as many people; fasting for almost one-third of the time; or walking about two-fifths of the distance. Moreover, the ritual condition was associated with increaseSs of approximately 25% and S 18% on the two happiness scales, over four times greater than the increases (5%, 4%) E R associated with the low-intensity condition. P Moreover, in accordance with previous research indicating that social support and N I collective engagement can modulate perceptions of physical exertion and enhance E emotional satisfaction (Deci & RyaLn, 2000; Schnall et al., 2008), we found that activities C performed in a group conteIxt were perceived as less difficult and more happiness- T inducing compared to thRe same activities performed individually. A Our findings extend the heuristic framing by suggesting practical applications for reframing challenging or unpleasant behaviors. Indeed, the ritualization of otherwise utilitarian actions may provide a powerful means of motivating beneficial behaviors both at the individual and the collective level (Xygalatas, 2024). For instance, could reframing weight-loss or medical diet programs in terms of ritual fasting aid in the adoption of healthier eating practices? Could rebranding tedious, often unrewarding repetitive activities, such as voting or recycling, as sacred rituals help promote civic engagement or environmental stewardship? If these seem like far-fetched ideas, we only need consider 17 ARTICLE IN PRESS that there is nothing intrinsically meaningful about the activities described in our vignettes. It is the framing and the context alone that makes these seemingly mundane activities seem more appealing and less appalling. It is worth noting that the effects of ritual in our study were stronger for older individuals across all models. In a rapidly secularizing world, this raises the question of whether the ritual stance may be losing relevance among younger generations. Cognitive theories of religion, however, argue that it is not. Rather than a purely cultural lens, the ritual stance is an intuitive way of looking at the world that sStems from evolved cognitive S predispositions and is therefore a recurrent feature of all human societies (Barrett & E R Lawson, 2001; Boyer, 2002; McCauley, 2013; McCauley & Lawson, 2002; Xygalatas, P 2016). Thus, while its particular forms and their relative appeal may vary according to N I local and generational trends and preferences, its overall presence is as pervasive as E ever. After all, it is precisely in thosLe parts of the world where participation in the liturgical C life of organized religions is rIapidly dropping that new forms of ritual expression appear T most forcefully, from NeRw Age movements and digital rituals to the ritualization of secular A domains such as college life, sports, or politics. Seen in this light, the aforementioned implications and potential applications of the ritual stance appear even more plausible. As a consequence of this, we expect that the ritual stance will not be confined to religious rituals. While religion has for much of human history claimed a monopoly on ceremony, ritual predates organized religion and extends far beyond it (Xygalatas, 2022b). There is likely nothing special about religious rituals. Although religious systems are very good at creating meaningful rituals, they are by no means the only domain where ritual happens. From families to nations and from sports to college life, virtually all levels 18 ARTICLE IN PRESS of social organization have their own rituals. Future research may examine how these domains fare comparatively in triggering the ritual stance. In addition to these cognitive perspectives, our findings may also speak to evolutionary debates on ritual. For instance, Costly Signaling Theory argues that the high costs often imposed on ritual practitioners (e.g. in the form of time and energy investments) can contribute to the stabilization of cooperation by functioning as honest displays of commitment (Irons, 2001), deterring free-riders who might not be willing to pay the price of admission (Bulbulia, 2012), and enhancing thSe perceived value of group S membership (Henrich, 2009). If, as our findings suggest, ritual costs are systematically E R underestimated in the eyes of potential practitioners, they will be more likely to participate. P Meanwhile, if these costs are underestimated in the eyes of the entire community, then N I practitioners may be under pressure to undertake even costlier displays of commitment E to sidestep the potential ambiguLity of subtler signals (Fischer & Xygalatas, 2014; C Xygalatas, 2022a; XygalatasI, Maňo, Bahna, et al., 2021). This escalation, in turn, may T help the receivers of thRe signal (community members who observe their performance) A circumvent borderline cases, i.e. situations where the sincerity of a participant’s commitment is ambiguous or unclear, thereby improving the signal-to-noise ratio and facilitating cooperative dynamics. In other words, by escalating the costs of rituals, practitioners can send a stronger signal of their commitment, reducing ambiguity in observers' judgments. Our study only examined religious insiders. However, it is a common anthropological observation that rituals, as arbitrary symbolic expressions, can be meaningful to insiders while appearing bizarre to outsiders. We therefore expect that the 19 ARTICLE IN PRESS effects we document here would be absent and possibly reversed if participants were to judge the same actions in the context of unfamiliar rituals. Further research may test this prediction. Our findings contribute to cognitive theories of ritual by offering empirical support for the distinct processing of ritual actions and their social and cultural underpinnings. Furthermore, they offer insights into how rituals, as culturally salient experiences, can endow actions with meaning, rendering them less daunting and more fulfilling. Finally, they speak to evolutionary perspectives on ritual as they pSertain to the assessment of S ritual costs. Taken together, these insights underscore the role of rituals in human E R societies as mechanisms for managing perceptions of costs and enhancing social P cohesion and emotional well-being. JSON: Name: ritual_frame_perception Title: Vignette-based randomized field experiment testing whether ritual framing alters perceived effort and affect during everyday actions Short Hypothesis: Framing an identical action as a ritual (vs. utilitarian) causes lower perceived difficulty and higher reported happiness during and after the action. Related Work: Prior work contrasts an 'instrumental stance' with a 'ritual stance' and shows that causally opaque, conventional actions are processed differently from utilitarian actions. Experimental and developmental studies indicate that observers parse ritualized actions as discrete, goal-like events, that children preferentially imitate ceremonial behavior with higher fidelity than instrumental actions, and that ritualized handling or presentation increases perceived object value and efficacy. Separate literature shows social context and support can reduce perceived effort and pain. Evolutionary and cultural theories propose that ritual signaling and high-fidelity transmission sustain cooperation. Limitations across these lines include reliance on lab-based or child-focused samples, limited field validation in culturally salient contexts, predominantly hypothetical or descriptive measures of ritual effects, sparse manipulation of objective effort intensity and social context simultaneously, and insufficient tests of whether framing effects translate into behavioral willingness rather than only reported perceptions. Cross-cultural generalizability and outsider/insider differences remain underexplored. Abstract: This project addresses whether adopting a ritual interpretive frame causally changes judgments of effort and affect for identical actions. We use a randomized, within-subject vignette design in a field sample to manipulate framing (ritual vs. utilitarian), action type, objective intensity, and social context while measuring perceived difficulty and happiness during and after the action. The main contribution is the quantification of the causal effect of ritual framing on subjective effort-relevant judgments and the characterization of its interaction with intensity and group context. Expected outcomes are (1) a measurable decrease in perceived difficulty and increase in reported happiness when actions are framed as ritual, (2) evidence that framing re-weights but does not eliminate sensitivity to objective intensity, and (3) an amplification of framing effects in collective contexts. Results will clarify whether the ritual stance operates as a cognitive heuristic that lowers perceived barriers to participation and inform broader questions about cultural transmission and motivation for costly behaviors. Experiments: Dataset: Field-collected responses from N=289 adult self-identified Hindu participants (within-subject design). Each subject sees 4 target vignettes (carrying, cooking, fasting, walking) x 2 intensity levels (low/high) x 2 framing conditions (ritual vs non-ritual) x 2 social contexts (alone vs group), randomized; practice items precede targets. Measures: three 0-10 VAS outcomes per vignette: happiness_during, happiness_after, difficulty. Covariates: age (continuous), sex (binary/multi), religiosity (4-pt), ritual_attendance (4-pt). Baselines: non-ritual framing is primary baseline; low-intensity non-ritual alone sets null comparison. Primary analysis: linear mixed-effects models (lmer) fit separately to each outcome with formula outcome ~ framing * intensity * group + age + sex + religiosity + (1|subject) + (1|activity_type). Report fixed-effect estimates, 95% CI, p-values, marginal and conditional R2, and Cohen's d for framing main effect. Model comparison: likelihood-ratio tests comparing nested models (with and without framing term). Multiple-testing: control false discovery rate at alpha=0.05. Secondary analyses: (a) include interaction terms framing*religiosity and framing*attendance; (b) Bayesian multilevel re-estimation (brms) to produce posterior distributions of framing effects; (c) compute percent change relative to baseline mean. Ablation/comparison studies: (1) Remove group context to test mediation by sociality (compare models with and without group); (2) Behavioral validation sub-study (N>=80): randomized offer of a real low-cost effortful task (lifting/carrying or timed repetitive task) with identical task but framed as ritual vs utilitarian; measure actual time on task, willingness to repeat, and self-report outcomes; compare hypothetical vignette ratings to observed behavior. Additional robustness checks: stratified analyses by age tertiles, by language of administration, and excluding participants who self-report other faiths. Pre-registration: analysis plan and power calculation pre-registered; target power 0.8 to detect small-to-medium effect (d=0.3) for within-subject framing effect. Risk Factors and Limitations: Self-report bias and demand characteristics: vignette responses can reflect perceived experimenter expectations rather than internal states. Ecological validity: hypothetical vignettes may not map onto real behavior; behavioral validation sub-study may still differ from natural ritual contexts. Cultural specificity: sample restricted to Hindu participants in one country limits external generalizability; unfamiliar-ritual or outsider responses may diverge. Sampling bias: convenience field recruitment may over-represent certain demographics; subgroup cell sizes (e.g., 'other' sex or low-frequency attendees) may be small. Confounding familiarity: ritual framing effects may be driven by familiarity or positive affect toward specific ceremonies rather than the abstract ritual stance. Translation and comprehension: multilingual administration risks subtle meaning shifts across languages. Measurement ceiling/floor effects: VAS responses may cluster, limiting sensitivity. Modeling assumptions: LMMs assume linearity and homoscedastic residuals; violation may bias estimates. Multiple comparisons: many interactions increase false-positive risk if not properly controlled. Ethical constraints: any follow-up manipulating real fasting or high-intensity tasks raises health and consent risks and may restrict experimental design. Computational limits: Bayesian re-estimation may require substantial compute for complex hierarchical models.
